assignment_tieins: CAP250 — entity-resolution / employer-name-matching module is a named contribution; must emit before/after join-coverage counts
A2 — verified-data instrument: every coverage number must trace; fuzzy matching must never auto-accept

beats.narration_text: Nik Bear Brown. Build it with a CLI, then take it apart.

beats.role_note: the stakes BEFORE the build begins — no terminal yet
beats.narration_text: Two tables, same company, different strings. The visa filing says 'Acme, Inc.' The funding record says 'ACME Incorporated.' A naive join misses the match and the candidate looking at sponsorship history sees 'Unknown' — a false negative about a company that sponsors every year. That's not a minor data quality issue: it's a decision made wrong, made invisible, and repeated for every candidate who looked at the same table. String normalization closes the gap without a model, and fuzzy matching after that requires a human in the loop.
beats.visual_intent: title card: 'same company, different string — the join miss that becomes a wrong decision'; PROBLEM beat, no terminal yet

build.suggested: suggested prompt: Two tables, same company, different strings. Acme, Inc. and ACME Incorporated. A naive join misses the match and the candidate sees Unknown.

beats.narration_text: In the terminal: ask Claude to write a normalize underscore employer function that lowercases, strips punctuation, and removes legal suffixes — inc, LLC, corp, ltd, co, incorporated, limited. Then join two fixture CSVs on the normalized name, print before and after join-coverage counts, the delta, and five rescued rows. Fuzzy matching is off by default: if the allow-fuzzy flag is passed, every proposed match prints as 'needs human confirmation' — it never auto-accepts.

beats.role_note: terminal (Onda) — read the output before running
beats.narration_text: Read the normalization function before running. Three steps, in order: lowercase, strip punctuation with a regex substitution, remove legal suffixes with a second regex, collapse whitespace. The join key is the normalized name — not the original, not a hash, the readable normalized string so you can inspect every rescued row by eye. That inspectability is the contract: every rescued match has to be verifiable without trusting the algorithm.

props.code:
# normalize_employer.py — Claude Code output
import re

LEGAL_SUFFIXES = re.compile(
    r"\b(inc|llc|corp|ltd|co|incorporated|limited)\b"
)

def normalize_employer(name: str) -> str:
    name = name.lower()
    name = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", name)   # strip punct
    name = LEGAL_SUFFIXES.sub("", name)      # drop suffixes
    return " ".join(name.split())            # collapse spaces

# join on the readable normalized key
df_dol["key"] = df_dol["employer"].apply(normalize_employer)
df_sec["key"] = df_sec["employer"].apply(normalize_employer)
merged = df_dol.merge(df_sec, on="key", how="inner")

beats.role_note: screen-recording — before/after coverage counts + rescued rows sample
beats.narration_text: Run it on the fixtures. Before normalization: sixty-one matches. After: eighty-nine. Twenty-eight rescued rows — companies that appeared in both tables with identical legal substance and different formatting. The sample prints: 'Acme, Inc.' and 'ACME Incorporated' now share a key. No fuzzy matching, no embedding distance, no model — just case, punctuation, and three regex substitutions. Every rescued row is readable and verifiable by a human in under a second.
beats.visual_intent: screen-recording: before/after counts printing (61 → 89, delta +28), 5 rescued rows showing exact string pairs that normalize to the same key

beats.role_note: terminal (Onda) — enable fuzzy and show a false positive
beats.narration_text: Now turn on allow-fuzzy and show a false positive. Ask Claude to add rapidfuzz to the unmatched rows with a similarity threshold of eighty-eight, printing every proposed match as 'needs human confirmation' with the score. Then deliberately show one false positive: two genuinely different firms with similar names. That false positive is why fuzzy matching must never run without a human sign-off.

props.command:
claude "Update normalize_employer.py:
add --allow-fuzzy flag: run rapidfuzz.fuzz.ratio>=88
on unmatched rows. Print each match as:
  NEEDS HUMAN CONFIRMATION: [A] | [B] (score: X)
Never auto-accept. Show one false positive:
two different firms with similar normalized names."

beats.narration_text: The join is the highest-leverage fix in a verified-data pipeline and the cheapest. Normalization moved coverage from sixty-one to eighty-nine without a model, without training data, without an API call. Fuzzy matching proposes — never accepts. The human sign-off is the gate. A join that fabricates a match — auto-accepting a fuzzy score — is worse than one that honestly reports 'Unknown.' Coverage you can't trace is not coverage.
beats.visual_intent: recap card: 'normalization: 61 → 89; fuzzy: propose, never accept'; the delta number large

build.suggested: suggested prompt: The join is the highest-leverage fix. Normalization: 61 to 89. Fuzzy matching proposes, never accepts. Coverage you can't trace is not coverage.

beats.narration_text: Your move: take any two tables you're joining on employer or company names. Run before-and-after counts on normalization alone. Report the delta and the rescued-row sample. If you're tempted to add fuzzy matching, write the human-confirmation step first — before any auto-accept logic — and keep it off by default.
